## Warm up 

What's the difference between a z and t distribution?

      
## Last time 

A teacher wants to know whether using a new study app causes students to be more likely to pass an exam.

The teacher has 100 students who agree to participate. She randomly assigns:

| Group        | Passed | Total |
| ------------ | -----: | ----: |
| Study App    |     42 |    50 |
| No Study App |     34 |    50 |

... and we both conducted a hypothesis test and created a confidence interval!

## Results 

Confidence Interval 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}_1 &= \frac{42}{50}=0.84 \\
\hat{p}_2 &= \frac{34}{50}=0.68 \\[4pt]
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 &= 0.16 \\[6pt]
SE &= \sqrt{
\frac{0.84(1-0.84)}{50}
+
\frac{0.68(1-0.68)}{50}
} \\[6pt]
&= 0.0864 \\[6pt]
95\%\ CI &= 0.16 \pm 1.96(0.0864) \\[4pt]
&= 0.16 \pm 0.1693 \\[4pt]
&=\boxed{(-0.0093,\ 0.3293)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Hypothesis Test 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

# Create standard normal distribution
data <- data.frame(
  z = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
)

data$y <- dnorm(data$z)

# Data for the shaded p-value region
shade <- subset(data, z >= 1.87)

ggplot(data, aes(x = z, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  
  # Shade the p-value
  geom_area(
    data = shade,
    aes(x = z, y = y),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Mark z = 1.87
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1.87,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Label
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.35,
    y = 0.08,
    label = "p-value",
    color = "steelblue",
    size = 5
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.87,
    y = 0.42,
    label = "z = 1.87",
    color = "red",
    size = 5
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Standard Normal Distribution",
    subtitle = "Right-tailed test",
    x = "z",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```


# Do my tests agree?

## Not really 

But here is why?

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Observed proportions
p1 <- 42/50
p2 <- 34/50
diff <- p1 - p2

# Null (pooled) SE
p_pool <- (42 + 34)/(50 + 50)

SE_null <- sqrt(
  p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1/50 + 1/50)
)

# CI SE
SE_CI <- sqrt(
  p1*(1-p1)/50 +
  p2*(1-p2)/50
)

# 95% CI
z_star <- 1.96
lower <- diff - z_star*SE_CI
upper <- diff + z_star*SE_CI

# Create x values
x <- seq(-0.15, 0.40, length.out = 1000)

# Data for both panels
df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    y = dnorm(x, 0, SE_null),
    Panel = "Hypothesis Test: Null Distribution"
  ),
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    y = dnorm(x, diff, SE_CI),
    Panel = "95% Confidence Interval"
  )
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
  
  # Shade p-value in null distribution
  geom_area(
    data = subset(
      df,
      Panel == "Hypothesis Test: Null Distribution" &
        x >= diff
    ),
    fill = "red",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  
  # Shade the 95% CI in the CI distribution
  geom_area(
    data = subset(
      df,
      Panel == "95% Confidence Interval" &
        x >= lower & x <= upper
    ),
    fill = "skyblue",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Null value = 0
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    color = "darkgreen",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Observed difference
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = diff,
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # CI endpoints
  geom_vline(
    data = data.frame(
      x = c(lower, upper),
      Panel = "95% Confidence Interval"
    ),
    aes(xintercept = x),
    color = "blue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  facet_wrap(~Panel, ncol = 1) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Why p < 0.05 but the 95% CI Contains 0",
    x = "Difference in Proportions",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```

## Summary 

A hypothesis test at a given $\alpha$ should have results that coincide with with a (1 - $\alpha$)% confidence interval ...

... IF the hypothesis test is two-sided.

There are special exceptions (like the one above) where our tests disagree.

## Last Time 

Suppose we want to test whether the mean home value differs between Wake County and Mecklenburg County. We'll compare 100 homes randomly selected homes in Wake County with 100 randomly selected homes in Mecklenburg County. The Wake County sample had a mean home value of \$461,300 with a sample standard deviation of \$120,000, while the Mecklenburg County sample had a mean home value of \$406,800 with a sample standard deviation of \$105,000.

-- Hypotheses? 

-- Assumptions? 

## CLT 

n > 30

[Let's talk about it](https://www.statcrunch.com/applets/type3&samplingdist)

## Hypotheses 

$Ho: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$

$Ha: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0$

$\bar{x_1} - \bar{x_2}$

$461,300 - 406,800 = 54,500$ 

## Sampling Distribution 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)

null_dist <- data.frame(
  difference = rnorm(
    10000,
    mean = 0,
    sd = 15910
  )
)

ggplot(null_dist, aes(x = difference)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 50,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution of Difference in Means Under Ho",
    x = "Difference in Sample Means ($)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


## Sampling Distribution{.smaller} 

**A linear combination of independent normal random variables is also normally distributed.**


$$
\bar{X}_W \sim N\left(\mu_W,\frac{\sigma_W^2}{n_W}\right)
$$

and

$$
\bar{X}_M \sim N\left(\mu_M,\frac{\sigma_M^2}{n_M}\right)
$$




Since both variables are normal, their linear combination is normal:

$$
\bar{X}_W-\bar{X}_M
\sim
N\left(
\mu_W-\mu_M,
\frac{\sigma_W^2}{n_W}+\frac{\sigma_M^2}{n_M}
\right)
$$

## Difference in proportions{.smaller} 

Conceptually, it's very similar for a difference in proportions!

... proportions are based on binomial/random-count data, so we use the Central Limit Theorem/normal approximation rather than saying the original observations are normally distributed.

$$
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
\approx
N\left(
p_1 - p_2,\,
\frac{p(1-p)}{n_1}
+
\frac{p(1-p)}{n_2}
\right)
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false

ggplot(null_dist, aes(x = difference)) +
  geom_histogram(
```

## test-statistic 

$\frac{\text{statistic - null value}}{\text{standard error}}$

And we know all of these! 

## test-statistic 

statistic - $461,300 - 406,800 = 54,500$ 

null value - 0 

$SE_{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}=\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$

What statistic are we calculating? t or z? 

# t 

## t

$$
t=
\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)_0}
{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
$$

# t 

$$
t=
\frac{461{,}300-406{,}800}
{\sqrt{
\frac{120{,}000^2}{100}
+
\frac{105{,}000^2}{100}
}} = 3.43
$$

Draw out the p-value! 

## t-distribution 

Every t-distribution is different! We need to specify the degrees of freedom.

## df{.smaller}

If you cannot access software, we recommend using degrees of freedom k equal to the smaller of 
$n_1$-1 and $n_2 - 1$. This approximation is appealing because it is conservative.

Software can use Welch–Satterthwaite:

$$
df=
\frac{
\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2
}{
\frac{\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}\right)^2}{n_1-1}
+
\frac{\left(\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2}{n_2-1}
}
$$

Welch–Satterthwaite: $df\approx193.5$

Conservative shortcut: df=99

## p-value guess

```{webr-r}
pt(3.43, 99, lower.tail = FALSE) * 2
```

# Questions 

## Confidence Interval{.smaller} 

Suppose we want to **estimate** whether the mean home value differs between Wake County and Mecklenburg County. We'll compare 100 homes randomly selected homes in Wake County with 100 randomly selected homes in Mecklenburg County. The Wake County sample had a mean home value of \$461,300 with a sample standard deviation of \$120,000, while the Mecklenburg County sample had a mean home value of \$406,800 with a sample standard deviation of \$105,000.

## Formula 

$(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t^*\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$

$(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2)\pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$

## t* 

$t^*$ is the critical value from the t-distribution that determines how many standard errors we move away from our observed difference in order to capture the desired confidence level.

The conservative estimate for our degrees of freedom is $n-1$ of the smaller group!

## t* 

We can find t-star using the following R code... and we know what this value should be close to!

```{webr-r}
qt(.975, 99, lower.tail = TRUE)
```

## Confidence Interval 

Calculate a 95% confidence interval 

## Confidence Interval 

$$
\begin{aligned}
(461{,}300-406{,}800)
&\pm 1.984\sqrt{
\frac{120{,}000^2}{100}
+
\frac{105{,}000^2}{100}
}\\
&=54{,}500\pm31{,}566\\
&=\boxed{(22{,}934,\ 86{,}066)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Interpret this in the context of the problem!
